analysis.one_liner: Exempts passive owners of oil facilities from liability for oil spills under the Oil Pollution Act.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it was referred to committee on April 1, 2022, sent to a subcommittee three days later, and died there when Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Oil Pollution Act of 1990, anyone who owns or operates an oil facility can be held responsible for cleaning up spills and paying related damages. This bill would carve out one group: people who own an interest in an oil exploration, production, or storage facility but take no part in running it. They would no longer be treated as responsible parties, unless they acquired their ownership stake specifically to dodge liability.
analysis.who_benefits: Landowners who hold an ownership stake in an oil well, tank, or storage site but leave the operation to an oil company — often farmers or homeowners who leased their land or inherited a mineral interest. They gain protection from being named liable for a spill they did not cause and cannot control.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Landowners with passive oil facility stakes

how_it_helps.text: The bill rewrites the definition of 'responsible party' for onshore facilities so that a person with an ownership interest in an oil exploration, development, production, or storage facility who does not participate in managing it is exempt from Oil Pollution Act liability [S3].
The exemption applies only if the person did not acquire the ownership interest in order to dodge liability under the Act, which is the bill's built-in guard against abuse [S3].
The CRS summary confirms the bill exempts non-participating owners of oil facilities from certain oil spill and pollution liability [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Victims of oil spills and the public. The circle of parties who can be made to pay for a spill gets smaller. If the operator cannot cover the full cost, the remaining burden falls on the federal Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund and, ultimately, taxpayers and affected communities rather than on every owner of the site.
analysis.who_pays_short: Spill victims and the cleanup fund

drawbacks.text: The bill shrinks the pool of parties liable for oil spill damage. If the operating company is insolvent or underinsured, one fewer deep pocket is available to victims and the public cleanup fund [S3].

The anti-abuse test — that the ownership stake was 'not designed to avoid liability' — requires someone to prove intent after the fact, which could let asset-shielding arrangements stand unless challenged [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is genuine and targeted: a passive landowner can today be swept into a multimillion-dollar spill case for an interest they inherited or leased and never managed. But the cost is a narrower liability net for oil pollution, and the anti-abuse clause puts the burden of proving intent on whoever challenges the arrangement. The trade is real but modest in scale.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its Coast Guard subcommittee, and no one ever brought it up for a hearing or vote before the two-year Congress expired.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Gibbs introduced the bill on April 1, 2022, joined by Reps. Balderson, McKinley, and Latta [S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure the day it was introduced [S5].
On April 4, 2022, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation, where it stayed [S5].
No further action was taken before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the current liability rules stay in place: passive owners of oil facilities remain reachable for spill damages, and spill victims keep that source of recovery. The federal cleanup fund and affected communities are spared a smaller pool of responsible parties, while passive landowners remain exposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Spill victims kept their sources of recovery

for.name: Rep. Bob Gibbs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 1, 2022, to exempt non-participating owners of oil facilities from Oil Pollution Act liability.

for.name: Reps. Balderson (R-OH), McKinley (R-WV), and Latta (R-OH)
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction; the bill drew 5 Republican cosponsors in total and no Democratic support.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee (Chair Peter DeFazio, D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it was referred to subcommittee and remained there until Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All four original sponsors and all 5 cosponsors were Republicans, and no Democrat signed on; the bill never advanced far enough for a recorded vote.

industries.industry: Oil and gas exploration and production
industries.note: The bill narrows the list of parties the industry answer to for spills, though operators still bear primary responsibility. Operators also benefit indirectly: landowners face less liability risk, which can make leasing land for drilling easier.
Ordinary landowners with a passive stake in an oil facility would no longer be treated as responsible parties for spills they did not cause or manage.

industries.industry: Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund / federal cleanup financing
industries.note: With fewer parties liable, more spill costs could fall on the industry-financed federal fund when an operator cannot pay, spreading costs more widely.
